q: What's the real difference between const and final in Dart?
a: They are exact synonyms with no practical difference whatsoever in Dart
const is compile-time; final is assigned once at runtime
const works only with numeric and String literals
final can be reassigned later, const cannot
e: const is a canonicalized compile-time constant. final is assigned once at runtime and may depend on computed values.

q: When do you actually need a Key on a widget?
a: To guarantee a globally unique id used when persisting the widget to a database
It forces a widget to rebuild more often
Keys are mandatory on every StatefulWidget
To preserve State when reordering identical widgets in lists
e: Keys help the reconciliation algorithm match elements and keep State when identical-typed widgets are added, removed or reordered.

q: Expanded vs Flexible inside a Row/Column — what's the difference?
a: Flexible always forces a tight fit while Expanded only suggests a preferred size to the parent
They are completely identical
Expanded only works in Column, Flexible only in Row
Expanded is Flexible with fit: tight — it fills all free space
e: Expanded forces the child to fill the space (FlexFit.tight). Flexible defaults to loose, so the child may be smaller than the space given.

q: A list of 10,000 items is janky. Best choice?
a: A Column in a SingleChildScrollView, which recycles offscreen rows automatically
ListView(children: [...]) with all widgets
ListView.builder — builds only visible items lazily
A Wrap holding every element
e: ListView.builder creates items lazily as you scroll. The others build all 10,000 widgets up front and kill performance.

q: Why isn't a change inside initState() visible after a Hot Reload?
a: You must clear the Gradle build cache and perform a full cold restart of the app
Hot Reload rebuilds build() but keeps State, so initState isn't re-run
Hot Reload calls initState twice
initState can never be edited
e: Hot Reload preserves State and only re-runs build(). initState runs again only on Hot Restart or when the widget is recreated.

q: What is the keyword late used for in Dart?
a: To schedule the variable's initializer to run later in the microtask event loop
To mark a deprecated field
To make a variable asynchronous
To defer initialization of a non-nullable variable
e: late lets you declare a non-nullable field without a value and initialize it later (lazily). Accessing it before init throws.

q: What problem does InheritedWidget solve?
a: It is the abstract base class that every StatefulWidget secretly extends under the hood
It inherits the parent's visual style
Efficient top-down data sharing with rebuild-on-change
It overrides the parent's build method
e: InheritedWidget gives O(1) access via dependOnInheritedWidgetOfExactType and rebuilds dependents. Provider, Theme and MediaQuery are built on it.

q: 'setState() called after dispose()' — most common cause?
a: A missing Key causes the element to be re-mounted at the wrong position in the tree
Using a const constructor
Too many widgets in the tree
An async callback calls setState after the widget is gone
e: A Future/Stream finishes after dispose. Guard with if (mounted) before setState, or cancel subscriptions and timers in dispose().

q: What's the core idea of the BLoC pattern?
a: Each widget instantiates and owns its own database controller for persistence
Use setState only, everywhere
Keep all state in global variables
Business logic is separated from UI via event/state streams
e: BLoC: UI sends Events, the component processes them and emits States. It separates logic from UI, is testable and reactive via Streams.

q: StatelessWidget vs StatefulWidget — the key difference?
a: Stateless widgets render animations faster because they skip the element lifecycle entirely
Stateful holds mutable state and updates via setState; Stateless is immutable
Stateful can't be used in lists
There's no difference in rebuilds
e: A StatelessWidget is fully described by its inputs. A StatefulWidget has a State object that survives rebuilds and updates via setState.

q: Heavy JSON parsing freezes the UI. Best fix?
a: Reduce how often setState is called so the framework can batch the parsing work
Wrap it in a Future without await
Move parsing to an Isolate (e.g. compute())
Add const constructors everywhere
e: Dart is single-threaded per isolate; async gives no parallelism for CPU work. compute() runs the work on a separate Isolate, freeing the UI thread.

q: What does the cascade operator ( .. ) do in Dart?
a: It null-checks the receiver before invoking each method in the whole chain
It makes a copy of the object
It concatenates two lists
It chains operations on one object and returns that object
e: Cascade .. invokes methods/setters on the same object and returns it: final p = Paint()..color = red..strokeWidth = 2;

q: Why mark widgets as const?
a: const eagerly caches network responses so repeated requests are skipped entirely
Flutter reuses one instance and skips its rebuild
It's just a lint rule, no runtime effect
const makes a widget interactive
e: A const widget is a canonical immutable instance. On a parent rebuild Flutter sees the same instance and skips rebuilding that subtree.

q: An animation repaints nearby static widgets. What helps?
a: Remove all Keys so the framework stops tracking element identity in the subtree
Wrap the animated part in a RepaintBoundary
Increase the number of setState calls
Switch StatelessWidget to StatefulWidget
e: RepaintBoundary creates a separate compositing layer, isolating the animated area's repaints from the rest of the tree.
